issues.legal_issue: A daughter in a Mitakshara coparcenary acquires coparcenary status by birth with the same rights and liabilities as a son, whether she was born before or after the amendment and whether her father was alive when it commenced.
material_facts: The connected disputes concerned daughters claiming shares in Mitakshara coparcenary property.
Some daughters were born before the amendment, and in some cases the father or another coparcener had died before it commenced.
The Court found that the daughters claiming rights were alive when the amendment commenced.
issues.conclusion: A daughter is a coparcener by birth in the same manner as a son, with equal rights and liabilities; her father need not have been alive when the amendment commenced.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6(1)(a)–(c) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, as substituted, confers coparcenary status by birth and equal rights and liabilities. The Court relied on the birthright and nature of Mitakshara coparcenary discussed in Sunil Kumar v. Ram Parkash and Controller of Estate Duty v. Alladi Kuppuswamy, and agreed with the relevant reasoning in Danamma @ Suman Surpur v. Amar. The contrary living-father requirement in Prakash v. Phulavati and Mangammal v. T.B. Raju was overruled.

predicates.mitakshara_coparcenary_exists: The property was held in a Mitakshara coparcenary.
predicates.daughter_alive_when_amendment_commenced: The daughter claiming the right was alive when the change in law commenced.
predicates.daughter_is_descendant_of_coparcener: The claimant was a daughter of a coparcener in that coparcenary.

issues.definition: When a daughter alive at commencement is a descendant in an existing Mitakshara coparcenary, she has the same coparcenary rights and liabilities as a son.

issues.legal_issue: The daughter’s newly recognized coparcenary rights may be claimed from the commencement of the amendment, while specified earlier dispositions and partitions remain protected.
material_facts: The amendment recognized daughters as coparceners based on birth, including daughters born before it commenced.
The disputes raised whether recognizing those rights would reopen earlier transactions involving coparcenary property.
The amendment expressly preserved specified dispositions, alienations, partitions, and testamentary dispositions made before the stated cutoff.
issues.conclusion: A daughter born earlier may claim the rights from the amendment’s commencement, but the specified earlier transactions are not invalidated or reopened.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6(1), including its proviso, and section 6(5) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, as substituted, govern the commencement and savings. The Court characterized the provision as retroactive in operation because the rights claimed from commencement depend on the antecedent fact of birth, not as retrospective reopening of settled transactions. It relied on the distinction between retrospective and retroactive operation discussed in Darshan Singh v. Ram Pal Singh and explained the operation of the amendment in light of G. Sekar v. Geetha.

predicates.coparcenary_property_claim: The proceeding concerns a claim to rights in coparcenary property.
predicates.daughter_claims_amended_right: A daughter claims the coparcenary rights recognized by the amended law.
predicates.transaction_completed_before_saving_cuto: A disposition, alienation, partition, or testamentary disposition covered by the statutory saving was completed before the specified cutoff.

issues.definition: When a daughter claims the newly recognized rights in coparcenary property, a covered transaction completed before the saving cutoff remains unaffected.

issues.legal_issue: A notional partition used to ascertain a deceased coparcener’s share does not itself effect an actual partition or end the coparcenary, and a pending partition proceeding must account for the daughter’s amended rights until actual partition is complete.
material_facts: Under the earlier law, a notional partition could be assumed to ascertain the share of a deceased coparcener in specified circumstances.
The connected disputes included partition proceedings in which preliminary decrees had been passed but final decrees or actual divisions by metes and bounds had not been completed.
The Court considered whether the notional partition or preliminary decree prevented daughters from receiving the benefit of the amended law.
issues.conclusion: The statutory fiction of partition only ascertains the deceased coparcener’s share and does not disrupt the coparcenary. A daughter’s equal share must be recognized in pending final-decree proceedings or appeals even if a preliminary decree has already been passed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered the earlier section 6 and its Explanation, and substituted section 6, including sections 6(1), 6(3), and 6(5). It relied on Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v. Hirabai Khandappa Magdum for the limited purpose of the notional-partition fiction; on S. Sai Reddy v. S. Narayana Reddy and Ganduri Koteshwaramma v. Chakiri Yanadi for the incompleteness of partition before a final decree; and on Phoolchand v. Gopal Lal and Prema v. Nanje Gowda concerning adjustment of shares when circumstances or law change before final decree. A preliminary decree declares shares but does not complete partition.

rule.if: pending_partition_proceeding and preliminary_decree_passed and actual_partition_incomplete and daughter_entitled_under_amended_law

predicates.pending_partition_proceeding: A suit or appeal concerning partition remained pending.
predicates.preliminary_decree_passed: The court had declared the parties’ shares in a preliminary decree.
predicates.actual_partition_incomplete: The property had not been finally divided and allotted by metes and bounds.
predicates.daughter_entitled_under_amended_law: A daughter was entitled to an equal coparcenary share under the amended law.

issues.definition: If a partition proceeding remains pending after a preliminary decree and actual division is incomplete, an entitled daughter’s equal share must be recognized before final partition.

issues.legal_issue: A claimed oral partition does not qualify as a protected partition merely on oral assertions or an unregistered memorandum, though it may be accepted exceptionally when strong public documentary evidence establishes a completed partition.
material_facts: The disputes raised claims that oral partitions or unregistered documents recording partitions had occurred before daughters asserted their amended rights.
The Court noted that such claims could be fabricated or used to defeat daughters’ rights.
The Court required a claimed exceptional oral partition to be supported by public documents and established as finally effected in a manner comparable to a court-ordered partition.
issues.conclusion: A plea of oral partition based on oral evidence alone must be rejected. It may be accepted only exceptionally where public documents and cogent evidence establish that partition was fully effected.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6(5) and its Explanation define the recognized modes of partition as a duly registered partition deed or a decree of a court. The Court relied on Kale v. Deputy Director of Consolidation for the principles governing family arrangements, and considered Chinthamani Ammal v. Nandgopal Gounder and Rukhmabai v. Laxminarayan on proof of partition and the possibility of sham documents. It held that the statutory definition imposes a heavy burden and that oral evidence alone is insufficient.

rule.if: daughter_claims_coparcenary_share and oral_partition_asserted and not (public_documentary_evidence and partition_fully_effected)

predicates.daughter_claims_coparcenary_share: A daughter claimed a share in coparcenary property.
predicates.oral_partition_asserted: A party relied on an oral partition to resist the daughter’s claim.
predicates.public_documentary_evidence: Contemporaneous or other cogent public documents supported the alleged partition.
predicates.partition_fully_effected: The evidence established that the property had been finally partitioned, rather than merely that an intention to separate had been expressed.

issues.definition: When an oral partition is asserted against a daughter’s coparcenary claim, it is rejected unless public documents and evidence establish that partition was fully effected.
